abstract: Leveraging precompetitive collaborations for rare diseasesPrecompetitive collaboration helps efficiently address challenges common to rare disease stakeholders, paving the way for improved diagnostics, treatment development and access programmes.Through examples, we highlight success factors and determine what is needed to enhance the field, helping to maximise patient benefits from 21st century science.The low prevalence and heterogeneous nature of rare diseases presents challenges in patient diagnosis, designing and conducting clinical development programmes, evidence generation approaches and medicines access implementation.To help mitigate these challenges, we describe how precompetitive collaborations can be part of the solution, illustrated through different real-world models and recommendations to derisk the process and advance the field.Precompetitive collaboration can occur in any part of the drug research and development life cycle, from medicine discovery to post-authorisation, creating non-proprietary solutions to common limitations without distorting competition.(p1) Interactions can be public (government and or not for profit)-private or private-private, covering rare disease scientific and clinical research, knowledge creation, standards-setting, tool development, infrastructure deployment, and generation and aggregation of data.Interactions involving multiple partners often occur through a convener and a mix of approaches including: Systems frameworks which establish the infrastructure for shared workspaces, project management, engaging key stakeholders, and disease-agnostic initiatives; Platform frameworks that establish shared technology platforms, data standardisation criteria, data collection standards, protocols; Disease-specific collaborations that promote some aspects of research for a specific disease.

title: Effector-cell-engaging bispecific antibodies for cancer therapeutics: Engineering precision immunity
abstract: The bispecific antibody (bsAb) is a novel immune therapeutic platform that consists of a single molecule that simultaneously binds two distinct antigens, tumor-associated antigens and immune effector cells, to enhance the targeted killing of tumor cells. bsAbs can target T cells and natural killer (NK) cells or macrophages through receptors such as CD3, CD16 or CD47 and generate strong, MHC-independent antitumor activity. This review outlines the evolution of effector-cell-engaging bsAb formats, such as BiTEs, DARTs, TandAbs and IgG-like constructs, along with engineering strategies to enhance Fc function, valency, half-life, safety and efficacy. It describes clinically validated T-cell engagers, new NK-cell- and macrophage-targeting bsAbs, trispecific NK engagers, tumor-activated and mRNA-encoded bsAbs, and combination strategies with checkpoint inhibitors and cellular therapies, highlighting their role in precision oncology.

title: Estimating and predicting clinical trial outcomes in China
abstract: Around a quarter of drug development now has a Chinese origin, yet China-specific success benchmarks and forecasting tools remain scarce. We analyze all nongeneric drug trials registered on China's national drug clinical trial registry from 2013 to 2025, benchmark phase-transition probabilities of success (PoSs)-where success denotes a program advancing to the next phase or to approval-and forecast trial outcomes with machine learning using structured registry features and Chinese text. China's overall phase I-to-approval PoS is below 30% across most therapeutic areas, while phase II-to-phase III transition rates run far above global benchmarks. In out-of-sample evaluations, random forests reach areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve approaching 80% and logistic regression approaches 70%, with the sponsor's track record and text-derived signals as key drivers.

title: Flavones in osteosarcoma: Molecular mechanisms, antitumor activity, and translational challenges
abstract: Osteosarcoma remains the most common primary malignant bone tumor, and survival has improved little over recent decades because of metastasis and therapeutic resistance. Flavones exhibit diverse anti-osteosarcoma activities by suppressing proliferation, inducing apoptosis, ferroptosis and autophagy, inhibiting metastasis, and modulating oncogenic signaling pathways, including PI3K-Akt, Wnt-β-catenin, STAT3, MAPK, and NF-κB. This review summarizes the cell-line-specific molecular mechanisms of representative flavones, critically evaluates current experimental limitations, and discusses strategies to improve clinical translation through nanotechnology-based delivery and combination therapy. Although clinical evidence remains lacking, flavones represent promising adjunctive candidates for overcoming chemoresistance and improving osteosarcoma treatment.

title: Synthetic lethality and context-selective DNA-damage response dependencies: from genetic vulnerability to pharmacological translation
abstract: Synthetic lethality has established DNA-damage response (DDR) dependencies as a major strategy for precision cancer therapy, exemplified by targeting BRCA1/2 and poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase (PARP). However, genetic dependency alone does not ensure pharmacological tractability or clinical utility. Emerging targets, including WRN, POLQ, USP1 and PARG, impose distinct requirements for ligandability, selectivity, target engagement, patient selection and the therapeutic window. A comparison of their structural biology, inhibitor chemotypes, SAR, pharmacodynamic strategies, resistance mechanisms and clinical development shows that successful translation requires matching a tumor-selective dependency to an experimentally validated, exposure-controllable pharmacological mechanism. This framework supports the rational prioritization of context-selective DDR dependencies beyond BRCA-PARP.

title: From implicit prioritization to auditable decisions in natural product drug discovery
abstract: Natural-product discovery increasingly benefits from metabolomics, high-resolution mass spectrometry, molecular networking, cheminformatics and artificial intelligence; but analytical capacity does not ensure explicit, reproducible decisions. We propose a framework for prospectively formalizing how evidence is translated into auditable experimental actions. Three recurring gaps are addressed: incomplete integration of sample metadata, conflation of analytical detection with molecular novelty and lack of explicit decision thresholds. A four-tier architecture links source authentication, reproducible chemical fingerprinting, orthogonal prioritization and definitive characterization through documented decision gates. An 'evidence ladder' separates molecular-identification confidence from chemical novelty, biological novelty and translational relevance. The framework is intended to make an existing, largely tacit decision process more transparent, comparable and testable across laboratories.

title: Pathway-driven target prioritisation in drug discovery
abstract: Genome-scale association studies and functional screens routinely implicate hundreds of candidate genes per disease, yet only a few will be clinically validated as drug targets. Choosing which to pursue is a central drug-discovery decision that depends on interpreting each candidate in its biological context. Curated pathway databases provide this context, while enrichment analysis applies it at scale, turning gene-level signals from genome-wide association, transcriptomic, proteomic and clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR) studies into mechanistic hypotheses for prioritisation. This review examines how pathway-based methods inform target prioritisation, the databases and tools available for this purpose, and why pathway co-membership should be viewed as a starting point for validation rather than as evidence of causal involvement.

title: Dark proteome and emerging technologies for functional characterization and drug discovery
abstract: Despite major advances in genomics and proteomics, a substantial portion of the human proteome remains poorly characterized and is commonly known as the 'dark proteome'. These understudied proteins often lack detailed structural, functional, and biochemical information, limiting our understanding of their biological roles and therapeutic potential. Recent developments in artificial intelligence (AI)-based structure prediction, cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM), functional genomics, and multi-omics technologies have provided new opportunities to explore this hidden region of the proteome. Characterizing the dark proteome could reveal novel therapeutic targets for cancer, neurodegenerative, metabolic, and rare genetic diseases. In this review, we summarize current knowledge of the dark proteome, highlight emerging experimental and computational approaches, discuss key challenges, and outline prospects for translating dark proteome discoveries into therapeutic applications.

title: Bridging the translational gap in drug repurposing for rare diseases: clinical success versus regulatory conversion
abstract: Repurposing of drugs to treat rare diseases (RDs) is vital, but the translational gap between clinical evidence and regulatory approval remains unquantified. Analysis of 47 clinical trials showed that 66% of completed studies met their primary or key secondary endpoints. Nevertheless, only 39% achieved marketing authorization (MA) by at least one major regulatory agency (32% by the European Medicines Agency [EMA], 32% by the US Food and Drug Administration [FDA], and 24% by both agencies). A marked 'Sponsor gap' exists: academics led 64% of trials, yet industry drove 75% (EMA) and 67% (FDA) of regulatory successes. When looking at Marketing Authorization Holders (MAHs), industry sponsors held 100% of EMA authorizations in this cohort. To bridge this translational divide, we propose a framework combining AI-driven screening and N-of-1 trials to optimize academic-industrial handoffs and harmonize regulatory pathways, accelerating approval for underserved patient populations.

title: The future of peptide ADMET prediction: Leveraging AI to unlock new possibilities
abstract: Peptide-based therapeutics hold substantial promise for treating diverse diseases, yet poor stability, limited permeability, rapid clearance and context-dependent behavior continue to hinder delivery and clinical translation. Today, artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to support early property evaluation and enable rapid screening and prioritization of candidate peptides. However, given these peptide-specific pharmacokinetic challenges, accurate prediction of peptide absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion and toxicity (ADMET) remains a key bottleneck, posing considerably greater challenges than conventional small-molecule ADMET prediction and therefore warranting a focused synthesis of recent advances. This review examines AI-driven peptide ADMET prediction, synthesizing methodological advances and limitations, including peptide-specific data scarcity, limited transferability and inadequate representations of modified peptides. It further outlines emerging directions, including interrelated ADMET modeling, class-specific peptide predictors and integration of AI with physiologically based pharmacokinetic models.

title: Drug discovery strategies targeting B7-H3 (CD276) in lung and gastric cancers: From biological validation to next-generation small molecules, biologics and cell-based immunotherapies
abstract: B7 homolog 3 protein (B7-H3, also known as CD276) has emerged as a promising immune checkpoint target because of its high expression in solid tumors, limited presence in normal tissues and roles in immune evasion and tumor progression. This review focuses on the biological and therapeutic relevance of B7-H3 in lung and gastric cancers, where it contributes to oncogenic signaling, epithelial-mesenchymal transition, metabolic reprogramming and therapy resistance. We highlight its structural biology, target validation and molecular mechanisms while critically assessing therapeutic strategies, including monoclonal antibodies, antibody-drug conjugates, bispecific antibodies, chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-based therapies and emerging small-molecule inhibitors. We also discuss biomarkers, medicinal chemistry and future directions for precision cancer therapy.

title: Erratum to “Major objections in EU medicines authorisation applications: an analysis of dossier submissions by small- and medium-sized enterprises” [Drug Discov. Today 31(4) (2026) 104721]
Challenges and progress in access to rare cancer drugs in China: Insights from clinical trials, availability and affordability
abstract: This study evaluated the development and accessibility of targeted therapies for 23 rare cancers in China. Clinical trials increased between 2013 and 2025 but have recently plateaued, with 12% terminated or suspended. Domestic enterprises now dominate trial activity, while trials of imported drugs have declined. As of 31 December 2025, 63 targeted-therapy indications had been approved globally, compared with 40 indications for 15 rare cancers in China, and eight rare cancers still lacked targeted treatments. The median monthly treatment cost was US$2165, substantially exceeding monthly disposable income per capita. Costs were significantly lower for drugs included in the National Reimbursement Drug List or those with generic alternatives. Despite progress, important gaps remain in R&D incentives, treatment availability and affordability.

title: 5-HT7 receptor as a potential therapeutic target in irritable bowel syndrome: Current insights and future perspectives
abstract: R in the gastrointestinal tract and highlights its potential for future IBS therapy.

title: Chemoproteomics in covalent cancer drug discovery
abstract: • Covalent drugs have re-emerged in oncology through sustained engagement of nucleophilic residues. • Chemoproteomics measures covalent target engagement, selectivity and off-target binding across the proteome. • FluoPol-, isoTOP/isoDTB- and SLC-ABPP support ligand discovery and selectivity profiling. • Site-selective cysteine chemistry helps distinguish reactive residues from those that regulate protein function. • Chemoproteomics guides the development of covalent degraders, molecular glues, ADC linkers and allosteric activators. Covalent small-molecule drugs have re-emerged as an important class of targeted therapeutics because they can sustain target engagement and exploit nucleophilic residues inaccessible to reversible ligands. However, covalent pharmacology has historically been constrained by concerns about nonspecific reactivity and limited ability to measure target engagement and selectivity in native biological systems. Competitive activity-based protein profiling and related chemoproteomic methods address this limitation by quantifying target occupancy, identifying unintended protein engagement and localizing modified residues across the proteome. These measurements provide a mechanistic framework for evaluating whether electrophilic ligands are selective enough to advance. Here, we review how chemoproteomics has strengthened the development of covalent cancer therapeutics by linking covalent engagement to selectivity, function and translational prioritization.

title: Strength of weakness in molecular interactions: toward transient medicines in drug discovery
abstract: Biological systems are governed by a myriad of molecular interactions, many of which remain poorly recognized. Growing evidence suggests that transient interactions (K diss > 1 µM) dominate the interactome and are crucial for dynamic molecular networks. By contrast, drug discovery has largely focused on high-affinity compounds that bind strongly to their targets. Although this strategy has delivered many successful medicines, exploiting transient interactions can offer new therapeutic opportunities, particularly for complex diseases. Transient medicines are characterized by rapid binding kinetics, concentration-driven activity and the potential for multi-target and multivalent engagement. Recognizing transient interactions as functionally important rather than biological noise could expand the drug discovery design space and establish transient medicines as a complement to current therapeutic strategies.

title: The endothelin system: a potential target for the treatment of type 2 diabetes mellitus and associated cardiometabolic complications
abstract: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) is characterized by insulin resistance (IR), metabolic dysfunction, and cardiovascular (CV) and renal complications. Endothelin-1 (ET-1) receptors are widely expressed in insulin-sensitive tissues, including adipose tissue, skeletal muscle, and liver, which are both sources and targets of ET-1 action. Dysregulated ET-1 signaling promotes IR, altered glucose and lipid metabolism, inflammation, oxidative stress, and vascular dysfunction, contributing to obesity, CV complications, and multiorgan injury. In this review, we examine the role of ET-1 in T2DM complications, the indirect modulation of the ET system by established antidiabetic therapies, and the therapeutic potential of directly targeting ET-1 receptors and inhibiting ET-1 overproduction. We further discuss translational challenges and opportunities for combination therapies, biomarker-guided interventions, and precision ET-targeted approaches in cardiometabolic disease.

title: Patient-based evidence in mechanism-based drug repurposing: Challenges and recommendations
abstract: Drug repurposing extends the therapeutic potential of existing drugs, with mechanism-based approaches increasingly being used to identify promising candidates. Decisions on their development and value should consider both clinical outcomes and patient-relevant benefits and burdens. Patient-based evidence (PBE), including patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) and qualitative research, can provide this evidence. We explored stakeholder perspectives on the use of PBE through a cross-sectional survey informed by the Measurement Instrument for Determinants of Innovations. Stakeholders considered PROMs and qualitative methods to be relevant, particularly when collected early. Key barriers included limited knowledge, lack of organisational resources and uncertainty about acceptance of qualitative evidence. Survey findings and experiences from three repurposing trials informed practical guidance for integrating PBE into mechanism-based drug repurposing.

title: Paradigm shift in the management of drug development projects: artificial-intelligence-enabled parallel scenario execution for managing uncertainty
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming project management beyond efficiency gains by enabling parallel scenario execution, in which multiple outcome-contingent deliverables are prepared before key uncertainty-resolving events and rapidly converged once results are revealed. By extending set-based concurrent engineering, this approach addresses traditional implementation barriers such as resource constraints and combinatorial complexity through large-scale AI-driven preparation and automation. Drawing on late-stage clinical development and regulatory submission workflows as an illustrative example, we show how parallel scenario execution can reduce post-event lead times, improve preparedness for low-probability outcomes, reduce replanning burden, and support more robust decision-making under uncertainty. We discuss implementation considerations, including scenario prioritization, governance, quality assurance, AI resource allocation, and the essential role of human oversight.

title: Agonist-informed antagonist discovery: Discovery approaches, medicinal chemistry insights, and design boundaries
abstract: In ligand optimization and receptor-targeted drug discovery, agonist scaffolds and ligand series often provide valuable starting points for the discovery of antagonists and inverse agonists. Such scaffolds typically possess validated target binding properties and prior functional characterization, enabling researchers to examine how local structural modifications alter ligand efficacy while preserving key binding interactions. Agonist-informed antagonist discovery can arise from the deliberate redesign of known agonist scaffolds, but it can also emerge through functional differentiation observed during structure-activity relationship studies, hit expansion, or analog evaluation. Drawing on representative cases across these discovery approaches, this review identifies three recurring structural factors: disruption of polar interactions, alteration of hydrophobic contacts, and changes in ligand spatial occupancy. On this basis, the review further discusses the core prerequisites and design boundaries that must be considered when evaluating the feasibility of this strategy. Together, these analyses can help medicinal chemists assess the design rationale, application opportunities, and limitations of using agonist scaffolds and ligand information in the discovery of antagonists.

title: Revisiting the potential of elongation factors as drug targets for pathogenic mycobacteria
abstract: Drug-resistant Mycobacterium tuberculosis and non-tuberculous mycobacteria infections are a threat to global healthcare. The scarcity of therapeutic options highlights the urgent necessity to discover efficacious drug targets and inhibitors. Protein synthesis has been clinically proven to be an excellent target for antibiotic development. Translation involves three well-defined steps: initiation, elongation and termination. The crucial elongation stage utilizes elongation factors (EFs: EF thermo unstable, EF thermo stable and EF G) that facilitate the sequential addition of amino acids. This review provides a perspective on the potential of mycobacterial EFs as innovative targets because of their vital role in translation, trans-translation and other alternative functions.

title: Plasmonic biosensor platforms for next-generation personalized medical diagnostics
abstract: The increasing healthcare burden demands precise diagnostics for early detection and longitudinal disease monitoring. Although conventional assays such as ELISA and PCR offer precision, they require intensive sample preparation, bulkier instrumentation and prolonged assay times. This review examines plasmonic biosensors as a transformative alternative for personalized and point-of-care diagnostics. We comprehensively examine recent advancements, such as the integration of nanomaterials, microfabrication strategies, advanced surface chemistry and prototype miniaturization, and consider examples for the detection of cancer biomarkers (microRNA-21 and alpha-fetoprotein), viral proteins (respiratory syncytial virus and SARS-CoV-2), and inflammatory biomarkers (C-reactive protein). Furthermore, we address the critical aspects that hinder the clinical translation of plasmonic biosensors. The review concludes that, despite significant laboratory-scale progress, standardized manufacturing, scalable nanofabrication and the inclusion of artificial intelligence/machine learning frameworks remain essential for the widespread utilization of plasmonic technology in personalized medicine and diagnostics.

title: New insights into FOX proteins in cancer
abstract: Forkhead box (FOX) proteins are transcription factors whose dysregulation drives tumor initiation, metastasis, and therapy resistance, yet their direction of effect is determined by cellular context rather than by their conserved DNA-binding domain. Applying explicit criteria across all 44 human members, we find context-dependence to be the modal behavior, reversing in some cases within a single indication. This creates an inversion for drug discovery: The one structurally tractable region is common to the whole family, whereas the regions conferring selectivity are the least characterized. We assess small-molecule inhibition, covalent ligand discovery, targeted degradation and indirect pathway modulation against the evidence for direct target engagement and identify nonconserved regulatory surfaces as the more promising route to selective FOX-directed agents.

title: Regulatory sandboxes for drug development: from uncertainty to structured evidence generation
abstract: Regulatory sandboxes for drug development offer a framework to address regulatory and legal uncertainty associated with novel sciences and technologies without compromising efficacy, safety, or quality. Here, we explore how regulatory sandboxes support structured evidence generation when existing regulatory and legal mechanisms are insufficient to address innovation. We synthesize concepts about when a sandbox is warranted, what evidence should be generated in a controlled setting, and how governance should be structured to protect patients and data while enabling responsible innovation. Our analysis highlights that sandbox value depends on explicitly managing uncertainty, conducting controlled experimentation, maintaining safeguards and oversight, and defining clear exit criteria linked to regulatory learning. A practical governance model is presented, together with a readiness framework covering regulatory knowability, value trade-offs, institutional capacity, infrastructure, and responsibility. When appropriately designed, regulatory sandboxes enable responsible innovation, credible learning, and better-informed regulatory decision-making while preserving regulatory standards.

title: Targeting IKZF2 with molecular glue degraders for cancer immunotherapy
abstract: Regulatory T cells (Tregs) restrain antitumor immunity and limit responses to immune checkpoint blockade (ICB). IKZF2 (Helios), a zinc-finger transcription factor enriched in Tregs, sustains suppressive programs under inflammatory conditions. Therefore, selective IKZF2 degradation has emerged as a strategy to reprogram intratumoral Tregs and enhance antitumor immunity. In this review, we summarize the biological rationale for IKZF2 targeting, the structural basis of cereblon (CRBN)-mediated IKZF2 recruitment and medicinal chemistry principles for improving neosubstrate selectivity. We highlight how degron recognition, CRBN surface remodelling and ternary-complex geometry shape potency, selectivity, off-target liability and translational opportunities for rational immunotherapy combinations.

title: Overview of screening assays used to evaluate PROTACs for cancer treatment
abstract: Proteolysis-targeting chimeras (PROTACs) are promising anticancer agents, but optimizing them requires screening strategies that go beyond simple target-degradation readouts. This review provides an overview of assays for evaluating anticancer PROTACs and classifies them by their role in the degradation pathway, including target binding and engagement, ternary complex formation, ubiquitination, target degradation and evaluation of anticancer activity in vitro and in vivo. The literature (articles published from 2020 to 2025) shows a strong dependence on degradation endpoints, especially western blotting, and relatively little use of direct ubiquitination assays, ternary complex measurements and quantitative kinetic methods. We highlight knowledge gaps and propose a staged screening framework that integrates mechanistic, quantitative, phenotypic and translational assays to advance the discovery of anticancer PROTACs.

title: Therapeutic peptide informatics in the artificial intelligence era: From curated resources to generative design
abstract: Therapeutic peptides are emerging as a powerful class of pharmaceuticals that combine the synthetic accessibility of small molecules with the specificity of biologics, yet poor stability and low oral bioavailability remain barriers. This review surveys an expanded, scope-defined set of 39 therapeutic peptide databases and 62 computational tools for activity prediction, physicochemical profiling, structural modeling and rational design. We highlight how machine learning and deep learning are accelerating data-driven peptide drug discovery and discuss the urgent need for standardized data frameworks and integrated evaluation platforms to bridge the gap between computational prediction and experimental validation.

title: ADMET all-inclusive: Accountability for the full end-to-end model life cycle is key to success
abstract: Drug discovery requires balancing efficacy with pharmacokinetic and safety properties. Although machine learning models for ADMET (absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion and toxicology) prediction are increasingly sophisticated, their impact is often limited by challenges in deployment, user adoption, interpretability and project-specific applicability. In this perspective, we describe Bayer's predicTeam approach, which assumes end-to-end responsibility for the prediction lifecycle, from endpoint selection and data curation to deployment, user training and performance monitoring. Key elements include close collaboration with experimental scientists, automated retraining workflows, structured user education and project-specific applicability reports. Drawing on more than a decade of experience, we argue that data quality, curation, governance and organizational accountability are often more important for impact than algorithmic innovation alone, particularly as AI-driven drug discovery continues to evolve.

title: Doing Drugs with AI
An IQ consortium cross-industry survey and perspective on AI/ML adoption in translational and ADME sciences
abstract: An industry-wide survey of 26 biopharmaceutical companies benchmarked artificial intelligence and machine learning (AI/ML) adoption in translational and ADME sciences. AI/ML is widely used in early discovery and small-molecule workflows but rarely the primary driver of decision making. Data quality and organizational readiness were identified as key barriers to adoption. Respondents highlighted molecular design and hybrid mechanistic-ML approaches as key opportunities. Beyond benchmarking adoption, this work provides cross-industry perspectives on the scientific, organizational and data foundations needed to scale impact through integrated workflows, shared benchmarks and collaborative translational decision-making.

title: From drug repurposing to antiviral activity expansion: building antiviral maps from multiple viral trees
abstract: We propose an evidence-weighted atlas for drug repurposing and antiviral activity expansion. Instead of using a universal viral phylogeny, our framework matches the way in which viruses are represented to the pharmacological question being asked. The atlas integrates five distinct layers: closely related viruses are represented in whole-genome trees, homologous drug targets in target-specific polymerase or protease trees, deeply diverged virion proteins in structure-derived trees, convergent cellular vulnerabilities in host-dependency networks, and a complementary view of chemical space, linking scaffold variation to breadth, potency and resistance liability, in antiviral structure-activity relationship trees. Candidate drug or activity transfers are filtered by pocket conservation, intracellular activation, tissue exposure, safety and resistance barriers. Successful and failed combinations calibrate the framework, which prioritizes the smallest justified 2-4-agent regimen for untreated viruses and Pathogen X.

title: Systematic review of EU and US product labels containing real world data in support of efficacy claims
abstract: Real-world evidence (RWE) is increasingly included in marketing authorization applications, and plays a growing role in regulatory decision-making. Although commonly included in product labels as safety information, its use for efficacy claims remains limited and randomized controlled trials (RCTs) remain the gold-standard. Regulatory guidance on the use of RWE is expanding, but a significant gap remains regarding its role in labeling, particularly for communicating drug effectiveness. This review examines how real-world evidence (RWE) has been used in many therapeutic areas to support efficacy claims in drug product labels approved by the US Food & Drug Administration (FDA) and the European Medicines Agency (EMA). A systematic search identified 173 brands that included RWE as primary efficacy evidence, as an external comparator to single-arm trials, or as supportive evidence alongside RCTs. This work offers insights for designing RWE studies that support labeling claims and inform regulatory guidance.

title: Blockbuster drugs and forecast accuracy: How sponsor type is associated with commercial success of FDA-approved medicines
abstract: We evaluated the commercial performance of 490 FDA-approved new molecular entities (NMEs) and biologic products approved from 2016 through 2025 against analyst forecasts, testing the hypothesis that only a small proportion of approved drugs have the potential to generate substantial returns for their sponsors. We demonstrate that analyst forecasts are subject to considerable limitations, with systematic overestimation of sales particularly prevalent for drugs with biotech sponsors. We further identify a strong association with large, established pharmaceutical companies and their ability to select or develop commercially successful products relative to smaller competitors and emerging companies. Large pharma achieved blockbuster (BB) or super-blockbuster (SBB) status for approximately 34% of their approved portfolio, compared to approximately 9% for medium pharma and approximately 2% for biotech sponsors.

title: The role and mechanism of heat shock proteins in the development of pulmonary arterial hypertension
abstract: Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) is a progressive pulmonary vascular disease characterized by increased pulmonary vascular resistance, right ventricular overload and premature death. Current therapies improve symptoms and hemodynamics but do not adequately reverse pulmonary vascular remodeling. Heat shock proteins (HSPs), key regulators of proteostasis and stress adaptation, are increasingly implicated in PAH pathogenesis. Among them, Hsp70, Hsp90 and Hsp110 have attracted particular interest because of their distinct roles in chaperone networks and vascular remodeling. This review summarizes the structural and functional features of these HSPs, their roles in PAH-associated remodeling and the therapeutic potential and challenges of HSP-targeted strategies.

title: From artificial intelligence promise to translational practice in drug discovery: Reproducibility, validation and evidence-based implementation
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) can support drug discovery, but benchmark performance alone does not establish experimental, operational or clinical benefit. This keynote review distinguishes predictive generalization, experimental confirmation, workflow utility and clinical outcomes, separating demonstrated failures from missing validation. We critically examine quantitative case studies of benchmark bias, prospective hit finding and clinical development, alongside data quality, reproducibility, uncertainty and governance. Practical recommendations link each intended use to appropriate comparators, evaluation designs and acceptance criteria. The aim is not to presume that AI fails to translate but to specify what evidence is needed to demonstrate reliable prospective use in drug discovery.

title: Advancing a drug-development program is not the same as de-risking it
AI-integrated iPSC multi-omics: advancing phenotype discovery and drug target identification in rare diseases
abstract: Rare diseases represent a major unmet medical need, yet the development of therapeutics for these diseases is limited by small patient cohorts, fragmented data, and uncertain disease mechanisms. Recent advances that combine patient-derived induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) models with multi-omics profiling and artificial intelligence offer a robust approach for phenotype definition and drug target identification that requires only minimal patient material. By integrating transcriptomic, proteomic, and metabolomic data, machine learning can produce disease-relevant molecular signatures, identify convergent pathway drivers, and prioritize druggable targets despite limited sample sizes. This short review highlights emerging in vitro models and AI-enabled workflows, discusses their strengths and limitations, and outlines practical strategies to accelerate drug discovery for rare diseases.

title: Patient access to cell and gene therapies in Europe: stakeholder perspectives on impeding factors across the medicine lifecycle
abstract: Cell (including tissue) and gene therapies (CGTs) have the potential to address unmet medical needs, yet few have successfully navigated the medicine lifecycle toward patient access in Europe because of impeding factors with possibly different stakeholder perspectives. Through a scoping review, we identified 991 document-stakeholder-theme combinations across 30 major themes of impeding factors and seven lifecycle categories. Most frequently reported themes were legislation & regulatory framework and capacity, resources, expertise, followed by uncertainty in regulatory & reimbursement assessments, quality requirements, and collaboration & coordination. Several stakeholders and product types were under-represented. We recommend active multistakeholder collaboration in designing legislation and capacity building to sustain patient access.

title: NR4A2: a next-generation drug target orchestrating dynamic gene regulation and protein interactions
abstract: Nuclear receptor (NR) subfamily 4 group A member 2 (NR4A2) is an orphan NR essential for the survival of midbrain dopaminergic neurons. Featuring a unique, dynamic collapsed ligand-binding domain (LBD), NR4A2 resides in the nucleus under basal conditions but undergoes nucleocytoplasmic shuttling under pathological triggers such as oxidative stress. Small molecules modulate NR4A2 by engaging diverse domains through dynamic LBP expansion, covalent latching, surface AF-2 targeting and retinoid X receptor (RXR) heterodimerization. Gene control exerted by NR4A2 reflects the extensive binding potential of its DNA-binding domain (DBD) with monomeric NGFI-B responsive elements (NBREs) and dimeric Nur response elements (NurREs). Here, we discuss a novel gene and protein interaction network of NR4A2 that is correlated with disease association data. This network mapping advances our understanding of NR4A2 across neurodegenerative and other systemic disorders, while highlighting key translational challenges in small-molecule drug discovery.

title: Advancing interleukin druggability: beyond ligandability toward therapeutic efficacy
abstract: Targeting interleukin (IL) signaling has long been constrained by the extensive, topologically flat and dynamic nature of cytokine-receptor interfaces. While monoclonal antibodies have validated these pathways clinically, achieving comparable efficacy with small molecules or non-antibody modalities demands overcoming steep pharmacokinetic and structural hurdles. In this review, we examine the translational trajectory across IL-17, IL-23, IL-1-family and IL-6 pathways by tracing compounds from in silico and biophysical hit identification to different stages of preclinical and clinical development. Rather than focusing merely on surface binding, we dissect the interplay between pocket dynamics (cryptic sites), modality selection (orally bioavailable macrocycles and traditional Rule-of-Five chemotypes) and the systemic liabilities of pathway crosstalk. These case studies provide pragmatic frameworks for converting structural ligandability into durable clinical outcomes.

title: PARP-1 selective inhibitors: A new direction in drug discovery to improve the therapeutic index of PARP-targeted cancer therapy
abstract: Poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase (PARP) inhibitors exploit homologous recombination deficiency, but are limited by hematological toxicity and poor discrimination between PARP1 and PARP2. Because PARP1 drives most antitumor PARylation and trapping, whereas PARP2 contributes to hematopoietic maintenance, selective PARP1 inhibition might widen the therapeutic window. Emerging agents, including saruparib and palacaparib, confirm that strong isoform selectivity can coexist with cellular target engagement, tissue exposure, and antitumor activity. However, biochemical selectivity alone is insufficient. Clinical differentiation requires matched comparisons of efficacy, unbound exposure, trapping, dose intensity, and marrow recovery. PARP1 selectivity remains a promising, but not yet proven, strategy for safer and more durable therapy.

title: Networked innovation in the new modality era: strategic insights from spin-offs and precision medicine
abstract: Despite major scientific advances, pharmaceutical R&D productivity remains a persistent challenge. This study motivates a network-centric model in which R&D performance can depend not only on firm-level scientific capabilities, but also increasingly on effective positioning and orchestration within innovation networks. Bibliometric analysis showed that previously reported network reconfiguration during the mid-2010s was temporally aligned with the rise of precision medicine. Approval-based analysis revealed the growing contribution of spin-offs and changing roles of large pharmaceutical companies, particularly for new modalities. An exploratory case analysis revealed distinct strategic trajectories in two spin-offs developing conventional or new modality products. Together, these observations converge to suggest strategic implications for pharmaceutical companies, investors, and policymakers navigating the era of precision medicine and new modalities.

title: Methadone: Historical success, modern challenges and lessons for opioid drug discovery
abstract: Methadone is a long-standing synthetic opioid that remains clinically important for pain management and opioid use disorder, yet it exemplifies the dual nature of opioid drug discovery. Despite its therapeutic success, methadone exhibits complex pharmacokinetics, polypharmacology and safety liabilities that have limited its broader clinical application. This review examines methadone as a case study to illustrate how chemical structure, stereochemistry, receptor pharmacology and pharmacokinetic properties collectively shape therapeutic outcomes and risk. We summarize key advances in methadone synthesis, structure-activity relationships, pharmacology and clinical limitations and discuss how lessons learned from methadone continue to inform modern opioid drug discovery. Particular emphasis is placed on balancing efficacy, duration of action and safety in the design of next-generation opioid therapeutics.

title: Aptamer-based therapeutics for malaria and neglected tropical diseases
abstract: Malaria and neglected tropical diseases (NTDs) affect over 1 billion people worldwide. Both disease categories share overlapping geographical regions, dependence on broad-spectrum treatments and common vectors, justifying their co-consideration as a unified therapeutic challenge. The broad-spectrum action of current treatments renders them susceptible to emerging drug resistance and off-target toxicity, which requires platforms that are specific yet effective across diverse pathogens. Aptamers are single-stranded oligonucleotides that fold into three-dimensional structures, enabling high-affinity binding to specific molecular targets and functioning as direct therapeutics or targeted delivery vehicles. We evaluate aptamers developed for malaria and NTDs, classify them into direct and delivery therapeutics and map candidates by preclinical validation stage, thereby constructing a translational road map that positions aptamers as a structurally adaptable platform addressing unmet treatment needs.

title: Incretin and nutrient-sensing GPCR therapeutics in type 2 diabetes: what target–modality–formulation matching explains
abstract: Receptor-directed therapeutics now dominate type 2 diabetes, yet their clinical value depends on more than target biology. This review proposes a pharmaceutics-centered framework spanning the receptors for glucagon-like peptide-1, glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide and glucagon, amylin co-agonism and selected nutrient-sensing receptors, it then tests against a defined cohort of 49 programs that reached Phase II in type 2 diabetes. Among arrests with a disclosed scientific cause, modality predominates; two-thirds of arrests were unexplained or attributed to portfolio decisions. Deliverability discriminates among comparable mechanisms, cannot raise a low receptor ceiling and is poorly served by the public record.

title: An EMA perspective on the regulatory approval of Waskyra®, the first gene therapy for the treatment of Wiskott–Aldrich Syndrome
abstract: European Union (EU) authorisation for the gene therapy medicinal product Waskyra® (etuvetidigene autotemcel; hereafter etu-cel) marks a milestone for patients living with Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome (WAS). The successful regulatory application for Waskyra by a non-profit organisation reflects not only the convincing scientific evidence supporting the authorisation, but also highlights that regulatory support is available from the European Medicines Agency (EMA) to help (small) developers manoeuvre the complexities of gene therapy medicinal product development for rare diseases. Here, we summarise the assessment by the EMA's Committees and present the key aspects underlying the positive outcome. Developers of innovative therapies addressing clear unmet medical needs are encouraged to seek early interaction with the EMA to help them design robust development programs and access supportive pathways that facilitate and accelerate development and evaluation.

title: Crosstalk between the cell cycle and ferroptosis in tumor cells
abstract: Cell-cycle regulation shapes ferroptosis through its influences on lipid metabolism, antioxidant defenses, and stress signaling. This review examines how p53, retinoblastoma protein, cyclin-dependent kinases, and DNA damage checkpoints influence ferroptosis in cancer. We reconcile the occurrence of both sensitization and resistance following cell cycle arrest by considering cellular state, arrest duration, lipid storage, redox status, and alternative defense pathways. Drug-tolerant persister cells are distinguished from other slowly proliferating cell populations. Proposed combination treatments remain preclinical, with translation constrained by pharmacokinetics, normal tissue toxicity, tumor heterogeneity, delivery, and unvalidated biomarkers. Functional metabolic assessment is therefore needed alongside cell cycle measurements to guide the future development of therapies that target the cell cycle and ferroptosis {AuQ: Edit OK?}.

title: UHRF1-mediated epigenetic dysregulation in tumors: Mechanisms, therapeutic resistance and targeted inhibitors
abstract: Ubiquitin-like with PHD and RING finger domains 1 (UHRF1) is a multifunctional epigenetic regulator that plays a critical role in tumorigenesis and cancer progression. However, the development of small-molecule inhibitors targeting UHRF1 remains in its early stages. This review provides a systematic overview of the molecular basis underlying the oncogenic functions of UHRF1, with a focus on its roles in epigenetic silencing, cell-cycle dysregulation, apoptosis suppression, metabolic reprogramming, signaling pathway dysregulation and immune evasion. Particular emphasis is placed on the role of UHRF1 in cancer therapeutic resistance, including resistance to chemotherapy, immunotherapy and radiotherapy. Additionally, we summarize recent advances in UHRF1-targeted small-molecule inhibitors, grade the reported compounds by the strength of the evidence for their binding mode and discuss their mechanisms of action, their therapeutic potential and the requirements for clinical translation.

title: Medicine’s missing memory: what AI’s mathematical breakthrough reveals about biomedicine
The Activity Wall in Alzheimer’s drug discovery: When potency optimization reaches its limits
abstract: Modern drug discovery attrition is often attributed to biological complexity or target invalidation. However, a core obstacle may lie in the industry’s asymmetric focus on maximizing binding affinity at the expense of holistic molecular quality, driven by a pervasive potency bias. This produces overengineered leads that collide with an ‘Activity Wall’, defined here as the multifactorial barrier that prevents chemical analogs from being optimized indefinitely, in which further affinity gains cease to translate into therapeutic success. By exploring chemical space through scaffold-based constellation plots and ligand lipophilic efficiency, we show how structural modifications improve potency primarily via lipophilicity inflation within established scaffolds. This is illustrated by analyzing small-molecule inhibitors of two key Alzheimer’s targets: beta-site APP cleaving enzyme 1 and the Tau protein.
